issue_context.title: Implement `apiserver_watch_cache_read_wait` metric
issue_context.body:
### What would you like to be added?

Part of https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/issues/2340

From https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/2340-Consistent-reads-from-cache/README.md#what-if-the-watch-cache-is-stale 


> Metric apiserver_watch_cache_read_wait will measure wait time experienced by reads for watch cache to become fresh. If user notices a latency request in they can use this metric to confirm that the issue is caused by watch cache.

For now posted as a "help wanted" issue, however if we cannot hit the timeline for 1.30 code freeze ([5th March](https://github.com/kubernetes/sig-release/tree/master/releases/release-1.30#summary)) I would take it over so we don't miss. Still issue is simple enough that it can be quickly implemented.

Implementation tips:
* Add a metric around waitUnitlFreshAndBlock method https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/f07b47c3d1e596f53640285afb0d53a81fe6f259/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/cacher/watch_cache.go#L441
* Metric should be a histogram with latency buckets similar to api latency
* Metric should have label for resource version.

### Why is this needed?

A way to monitor watch cache impact on request latency.

review_comments: Wondering whether it would make sense to record the metric only when `w.resourceVersion < resourceVersion ` holds true? Otherwise, it means we actually didn't wait and the cache was fresh, right?

I am seeing two scenarios for this metrics:
1. etcd not being able to keep up with read requests would be detected by a general increase in `read_wait_seconds`
2. a specific watch cache being clogged would be detected via `read_wait_seconds{resource="cloggedResource"}`

Is that correct?

Also in both cases the expected action from an admin would be to disable the feature flag right?

The reason I am asking is because I am wondering if we really need the `resource` label here.
The (2) case is the main one we're worried about. So yes - understanding that only some resource is affected is useful imho.
I think that kas permits configuring a separate etcd instance per resource. In such a configuration knowing that `events` resource behave differently that the other resources would be valuable.
No, it looks okay to me.
